section.title: The Wife of Noble Character
section.sectionRationale: The book closes with a complete acrostic poem, each of its twenty-two lines beginning with the successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph to tav, forming a full, ordered portrait of wisdom embodied in a working, generous, strong, and God-fearing life. It answers Lady Wisdom's call in chapters 1 to 9 with a sustained picture of wisdom lived out in the ordinary labor of a household.
section.thesis: Wisdom, praised abstractly throughout the book, is here shown fully embodied: tireless in work, generous to the poor, clothed in strength and dignity, wise in speech, and honored above all not for charm or beauty but for fearing the LORD.
section.frameNote: Six clusters follow the Hebrew acrostic's flow: her worth beyond rubies; her hands at tireless work; her generosity and preparedness for hard seasons; her husband's honor and her own strength and dignity; her wisdom and watchful care of her household; her family's praise and the fear of the LORD that outlasts charm.

units.label: Her worth beyond rubies
units.note: the heart of her husband trusts in her

verses.text: A wife of {{chayil|noble character}}, who can find? She is far more precious than rubies.
The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value.
She brings him good and not harm all the days of her life.

units.label: Her hands at tireless work
units.note: she rises while it is still night

verses.text: She selects wool and flax and works with eager hands.
She is like the merchant ships, bringing her food from afar.
She rises while it is still night to provide food for her household and portions for her maidservants.
She appraises a field and buys it; from her earnings she plants a vineyard.
She girds herself with strength and shows that her arms are strong.
She sees that her gain is good, and her lamp is not extinguished at night.
She stretches out her {{yad|hands}} to the distaff and grasps the spindle with her fingers.

units.label: Her generosity and preparedness
units.note: she opens her arms to the poor

verses.text: She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
When it snows, she has no fear for her household, for they are all clothed in scarlet.
She makes coverings for her bed; her clothing is fine linen and purple.

units.label: Her husband's honor and her own strength
units.note: she laughs at the days to come

verses.text: Her husband is known at the city gate, where he sits among the elders of the land.
She makes linen garments and sells them; she delivers sashes to the merchants.
Strength and honor are her clothing, and she can laugh at the days to come.

units.label: Her wisdom and watchful care
units.note: faithful instruction is on her tongue

verses.text: She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue.
She watches over the affairs of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness.

units.label: Her family's praise
units.note: a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised

verses.text: Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband praises her as well:
"Many daughters have done noble things, but you surpass them all!"
Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who {{yirah|fears}} the LORD is to be praised.
Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates.

chayil.gloss: Strength, valor, noble or excellent character, the same word used of mighty warriors and of Ruth, called an eshet chayil in Ruth 3:11. It names capable, valorous strength of character rather than mere social status, framing the whole poem as a portrait of active, strong virtue, not passive refinement.

yad.gloss: Hand, used throughout this poem, verses 13, 16, 19, 20, and 31, to picture tireless, skillful, generous labor. The repetition of hands at work, spinning, planting, giving, forms one of the poem's central threads, tying wisdom directly to diligent, practical action rather than abstract reflection.

yirah.gloss: Fear, reverent awe. Verse 30 sets this fear of the LORD against charm and beauty, both of which fade, as the one quality truly worth praising, closing the whole book of Proverbs on the same note it opened with in 1:7, the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.

basic.context: The book of Proverbs closes not with another saying but with a sustained poem, twenty-two lines long, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, painting a complete portrait of a woman whose strength, diligence, generosity, and wisdom embody everything the book has praised. She works tirelessly from before dawn, trades shrewdly, gives generously to the poor, speaks with wisdom, and is praised by her whole household, but her deepest praise is reserved for fearing the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: This acrostic is a poetic portrait, not a checklist, and its structure, moving through the entire Hebrew alphabet, signals completeness, a full picture of wisdom lived out, not a literal daily itinerary any one woman must reproduce. Read this way, the poem celebrates strong, capable, wise living rather than imposing a narrow domestic ideal that would burden or shame women who cannot match every detail.
basic.originalLanguages: Chayil, verse 10, names valorous, capable strength of character, the same word used of mighty soldiers and of Ruth, called an eshet chayil in Ruth 3:11, so the poem's opening line already frames this woman as strong and excellent, not merely decorative. Yad, hand, recurs throughout, verses 13, 16, 19, 20, and 31, binding the whole poem to tireless, skillful, generous action. And yirah, fear of the LORD, verse 30, closes the book on the same note it opened with in 1:7, tying this entire portrait back to reverence for God as the true root of all the wisdom it displays.
basic.typology: This poem answers and completes the personified Lady Wisdom of Proverbs 1 to 9, who called out in the streets inviting all to feast at her table; here wisdom is shown fully at home, embodied in a life of tireless, generous, God-fearing labor. The poem's praise of a life whose works speak for themselves at the gates, verse 31, anticipates Christ's own teaching that wisdom, and faith, are proved by their fruit, Matthew 7:16-20.
basic.christ: This closing poem's vision of wisdom embodied in tireless service, generosity to the poor, and fearless strength anticipates Christ, who is Himself the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, and whose own life was marked by exactly this pattern, tireless labor for others, generosity to the needy, and a reverence for the Father that never wavered. And the poem's insistence that charm and beauty fade while the fear of the LORD alone deserves lasting praise, verse 30, points to the deeper, lasting beauty of a life hidden in Christ, whose worth is not cosmetic but rooted in reverence for God, 1 Peter 3:3-4.
basic.god: God is the one this whole portrait ultimately honors, since the woman's crowning quality is not her strength, business skill, or family's praise but that she fears the LORD, verse 30, the very fear the whole book of Proverbs names as wisdom's beginning, 1:7. Every other quality in the poem, diligence, generosity, dignity, wisdom, flows from and returns to that reverence, showing that character rooted in God, not outward achievement alone, is what God finally praises.
basic.crossReferences: Ruth 3:11 calls Ruth an eshet chayil, the same phrase opening this poem in 31:10. 1 Corinthians 1:24 names Christ the wisdom of God, the fuller embodiment this poem anticipates. 1 Peter 3:3-4 echoes verse 30's contrast between fading outward charm and lasting inward worth. Matthew 7:16-20 echoes the poem's closing claim that works praise a life, verse 31.
basic.oneStory: This closing acrostic embodies everything Proverbs has praised, wisdom lived out in tireless work, generosity, strength, and above all the fear of the LORD that outlasts fading charm. The whole book's search for wisdom finds its fullest embodiment not merely in this poem but in Christ, the wisdom of God, whose life of tireless self-giving love is the pattern every reader, man or woman, is ultimately called to reflect.

context.literary:
Proverbs 31:10-31 is the only extended poem in the book built on the alphabet. Each of its twenty-two verses opens with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from the first, aleph, in verse 10 to the last, tav, in verse 31, as the BSB footnote on verse 10 says. An acrostic is a statement of fullness. Psalm 119, Psalm 145 and the first four chapters of Lamentations use the same device, and in each case the idea is the whole range of the subject, from A to Z. This woman is wisdom from A to Z.

The poem is framed. It opens with a question, 'who can find?', verse 10, and closes with a call to praise, 'Give her the fruit of her hands', verse 31, so that a search ends in an award ceremony. In between it moves in a loose chiasm. The early verses speak of the husband's trust and the woman's work at home and market. The centre around verses 20 to 22 turns to her open hands for the poor and the well-clothed household. The later verses return to her husband at the gate and her children, and her own character: strength, honour, laughter and teaching.

The poem is also a deliberate answer to the rest of the book. In Proverbs 1 to 9, Wisdom is a woman who builds her house, mixes her wine and calls from the heights, Proverbs 9:1-6. Folly is a loud woman who knows nothing, Proverbs 9:13. Here, at the end, Wisdom becomes a real person in a real household. The language of the poem is full of images of war and trade: 'strength', 'merchant ships', 'spoil' or gain in verse 11, a field bought and a vineyard planted. These are the words of the heroic world applied to the ordinary tasks of the home.

The last two lines show how the poem works. Verse 30 gives the reason for all the praise, and it is not the woman's skill but her fear of the LORD. Verse 31 then returns to the hands and the gates. The poem ends by saying that the proof of a life is in what it does and that the whole community can see it.
context.historical:
The household described here is a large, productive estate in Israel's agrarian world, not a small family unit as many modern readers imagine. She has maidservants, verse 15, she can buy land, verse 16, and she trades goods with merchants, verse 24. Wool and flax, verse 13, were the two chief fibres of the region, and spinning with distaff and spindle, verse 19, was daily work for women. Cloth was a major commodity, and Acts 16:14 shows a woman of Thyatira dealing in purple cloth two thousand years ago. The 'scarlet' and 'purple' of verses 21 and 22 were costly dyes; the BSB footnote on verse 21 notes the Hebrew could also be read 'doubly clothed', which would mean well wrapped against the winter cold.

The poem does not say she works at the cost of her husband's place. He sits at the city gate, verse 23, the place where elders heard cases and decided public matters. The gate is also where her works are finally praised, verse 31. The husband's reputation is built on the stability of a household that frees him for public service, and she herself is not hidden: her trade is public, her decisions are her own and she buys and plants without asking leave.

The cultural background also includes the high regard for mothers in Israel's wisdom tradition. Proverbs 1:8 tells a son not to forsake his mother's teaching, and the previous section of the chapter is a mother's oracle to a king. The 'instruction' on this woman's tongue in verse 26 is therefore not small talk; it is the same teaching, torah, that the book has valued from the start.

The poem was probably meant to be learned. Acrostics are easy to memorise, and many readers have taken it as a song that young men learned when looking for a wife, or that a husband might sing at home. It may also have been addressed to young women. The text does not say, and nothing here depends on it. What is clear is that it was shaped to be repeated, to fix in the memory a picture of what a lifetime of wisdom looks like.
context.canonical:
Within Proverbs the poem is the last page of the book, and it echoes the first. The 'fear of the LORD' that begins knowledge in Proverbs 1:7 and wisdom in Proverbs 9:10 is the quality that Proverbs 31:30 uses to crown the woman. The woman who is 'more precious than rubies' in verse 10 is a living version of Wisdom herself, who is 'more precious than rubies' in Proverbs 3:15 and 8:11. A man who finds her finds what Proverbs 18:22 calls a good thing and favour from the LORD, and she is her husband's crown, Proverbs 12:4, in contrast to the quarrelsome wife of Proverbs 21:9.

Outside Proverbs, the phrase that opens the poem appears in Ruth 3:11, where Boaz tells Ruth that all his fellow townspeople know that she is a woman of noble character. Ruth is a foreigner, a widow and a gleaner, and she earns this title by loyalty and labour. The title, then, is not limited to wealthy or well-born women. Psalm 112, which also celebrates the one who fears the LORD, describes a household of lasting blessing, and Psalm 128:3 speaks of a wife as a fruitful vine in the house.

The New Testament shows the same character at work. Dorcas, 'always occupied with works of kindness and charity', is remembered in Acts 9:36-39 by the widows weeping over the clothes she had made. Priscilla helped to teach Apollos, Acts 18:26. Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church and 'a great help to many people', Romans 16:1-2. First Timothy 5:10 lists a widow's good deeds in language close to the poem's: raising children, hospitality, relief for the afflicted and devotion to every good work. Titus 2:3-5 speaks of teachers of good who train others in the household. Peter's contrast between outward adornment and the 'unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit', 1 Peter 3:3-4, repeats the logic of verse 30.

Finally the Bible's closing images pick up the picture of the clothed bride. In Revelation 19:7-8 the bride of the Lamb is given fine linen, which is the righteous acts of the saints, and in Revelation 21:2 she is adorned for her husband.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The compiler ended Proverbs with this poem so that the book's long argument would not stay abstract. For thirty chapters the reader has been told what wisdom is, what it costs and what it protects against. Here he is shown a life in which it has taken root. The first hearers were meant to learn that wisdom is not a mood or a clever phrase but a way of spending days, and that it produces a particular kind of beauty: dependable, generous, brave and unafraid of the future.

The poem is also addressed to men who must choose a companion and to women who must choose who to become. To the young man it says that the thing worth seeking is not charm or beauty but character, and that such character is rare, 'who can find?'. To the young woman it says the same, and offers her a standard of dignity and agency that is far from the picture of passive ornament. The phrase 'noble character' sets her among the strong.

The poem is meant to be read as the book's last word on wisdom lived out. Verse 30 makes the root clear: the fear of the LORD. Everything else is fruit. The author wanted the community to see that the difference between a wise household and a foolish one is not wealth or luck but an inner reverence that shows itself in work, mercy and speech.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem describes. It contains almost no commands except the closing call in verse 31 to give her the fruit of her hands and let her works praise her. Everything else is a portrait. That makes it unsafe to turn the verses into a list of tasks a woman must do, as though every wife must buy a field, trade in cloth and be up before dawn. The poem names a person living in a particular economy, and its form, an acrostic of twenty-two lines, signals that it is a composite ideal, not a daily schedule. Many wise women will never plant a vineyard and many will do things the poem never mentions.

The principles do carry across. Diligence, wise management, generosity to the poor, strength of mind, careful speech and reverent fear of the LORD are things the whole Bible asks of every believer, man or woman. The poem is helpful when it is read as a picture of wisdom in action, not as a template that measures one woman against another. It is harmful when it is used to shame women whose circumstances differ, or to excuse husbands from the same character. The best use is the poem's own: to praise, as verse 31 does, those whose lives show the fruit of the fear of the LORD.

debates.question: Is the woman of the poem a real person, an ideal, or Wisdom herself?

views.label: An ideal portrait of a real kind of woman
views.case: The acrostic form, with its sense of completeness, and the way no one person could do all the tasks in the poem, suggest a composite picture. The poem begins as a question, 'who can find?', verse 10, which treats her as rare and valuable, not as a standard every woman is expected to meet. This is the most common reading.

views.label: Wisdom personified
views.case: Because Proverbs 1 to 9 personifies Wisdom as a woman, and because this woman is 'more precious than rubies' as Wisdom is in Proverbs 3:15, some readers see Lady Wisdom herself in the poem. The vocabulary is also shared: she builds a household as Wisdom builds her house, Proverbs 9:1. The danger is that the poem's practical tasks, such as spinning and trading, are then treated only as symbols.

views.label: Both: wisdom made flesh in a woman
views.case: A third reading holds the two together: the poem shows what Wisdom looks like when she takes a body and a household, and so it is both a concrete portrait and the book's closing image of Wisdom. This fits the way the book has used female figures to teach about wisdom and folly.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the root of the portrait is the fear of the LORD, and that it should be read as praise and instruction rather than as a rule. The poem calls every reader to ask what a life shaped by wisdom looks like in its own household and work.

debates.question: How should the poem be applied to women and men today?

views.label: As a model of domestic virtue for women
views.case: Some stress the household setting and take the poem as a charge to women to manage the home, care for the family and speak with kindness. They point to Titus 2:3-5 and to the husband's trust in verse 11. The strength of this reading is that it honours the work of the home as a high calling.

views.label: As a picture of wisdom for any believer
views.case: Others note that the woman's commerce, property dealings and community leadership go far beyond the home, and that the virtues of the poem, such as work, mercy, courage and wise speech, are the same ones asked of everyone in Proverbs. The honour given her is for character, not role.

views.label: As a pointer to Christ and the church
views.case: A further tradition reads the poem as a picture of the church, the bride, or of the faithful soul clothed with the Lord, with echoes in Revelation 19:7-8. This is a devotional extension, not a claim about the author's primary meaning.

debates.bearing: The text itself praises strength, wisdom and generosity, and it never sets her worth by any one task. Whatever one's view of roles, the poem is safest read as praise of character that every believer should seek.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word of the poem is eshet, 'wife' or 'woman', followed by chayil. The second word is a wide-ranging noun meaning strength, ability, wealth or an army. The same word is used in Exodus 18:21 for the capable men Moses was to choose as judges, and Proverbs 12:4 uses the same phrase for the wife who is her husband's crown. The best English rendering is 'a woman of strength' or 'a capable woman'; 'noble character' catches the moral weight but may lose the sense of competence. In Ruth 3:11, Boaz uses the identical phrase of Ruth.

The question 'who can find?' uses the verb matsa, to find. It is the verb Proverbs 18:22 uses for the man who 'finds' a wife and Proverbs 3:13 uses for the man who 'finds' wisdom. The poem therefore opens by reusing the language of the quest for wisdom.

Verse 11 says her husband 'trusts' in her, from batach, a verb that elsewhere describes trust in God. He lacks no shalal, a word usually meaning plunder or spoil, here used of gain. The warrior vocabulary shows that her management brings in what a conqueror might bring home.

In verse 25, 'she can laugh at the days to come'. The verb tsachaq is to laugh, and the laugh is not carelessness but confidence. She has prepared for snow, verse 21, and she is not afraid of the future because she has spent her days well.

Verse 26 says 'faithful instruction is on her tongue'. The Hebrew is torat chesed, literally 'the instruction of covenant kindness'. Torah is the word for the teaching of the law and of parents, and chesed is the loyal love by which God binds Himself to His people. Her words carry both. She teaches, and what she teaches is shaped by kindness.

Verse 27 says she 'watches over' the affairs of her household. The participle is related to the verb tsaphah, which is the word for a watchman on the wall. She stands guard over the house.

Verse 30 is full of wordplay. 'Charm is deceptive', sheqer, a word for falsehood, and 'beauty is fleeting', literally hevel, the 'breath' or 'vapour' that is the keynote word of Ecclesiastes. The woman who 'fears the LORD' is to be praised, from halal, the root of 'Hallelujah'. The contrast is between what fades like a breath and what earns the verb we use for worshipping God.

Verse 31 closes with 'the fruit of her hands', pri yadeha. Fruit is a recurring image in Proverbs, as in 'the fruit of the righteous is a tree of life', Proverbs 11:30. The hands that worked throughout the poem are at last given their reward.

typology.type: Wisdom made visible in a household, Proverbs 31:10-31
typology.fulfillment: Lady Wisdom built her house and invited the simple to her table in Proverbs 9:1-6. In this poem that wisdom has a body and a home. Jesus is the greater fulfilment, for Paul calls Him the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, and in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom, Colossians 2:3. The woman shows wisdom at work in one household, while Christ builds the household of God, Hebrews 3:6. The correspondence is in the pattern, not a claim that the poem is secretly about Jesus, and the type falls short because the woman's wisdom is learned while His is original.

typology.type: The clothed and adorned bride, Proverbs 31:22, 25
typology.fulfillment: The woman is clothed in fine linen and purple, and 'strength and honor are her clothing'. In the Bible's last chapters the bride of the Lamb is given 'fine linen, bright and pure,' which is the righteous acts of the saints, Revelation 19:7-8, and the new Jerusalem is adorned as a bride for her husband, Revelation 21:2. The church is presented to Christ 'without stain or wrinkle', Ephesians 5:27. The correspondence is one of image, not a prediction, and the escalation is that the clothing of the church is given by the Bridegroom, who cleanses her Himself.

typology.type: The open hand for the poor, Proverbs 31:20
typology.fulfillment: She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out to the needy. In Jesus the open hand becomes the pierced hand. He touched lepers, fed crowds and finally stretched out His arms on the cross, giving Himself for those who could never repay, Mark 10:45. In Matthew 25:35-40 He says that those who clothed and fed the least of His brothers did it for Him. The type is surpassed in what is given: she gives from her earnings, but He gives His life.

typology.type: The one who laughs at the days to come, Proverbs 31:25
typology.fulfillment: Her confidence about the future is rooted in preparation and the fear of the LORD, not in guesswork. The fuller form of that confidence is the believer's hope in Christ, who has defeated death, so that Paul can ask where its sting is, 1 Corinthians 15:55-57. The woman's laughter is a sign of a heart that does not fear the winter; the resurrection is the ground that finally secures it.

study.christ:
The poem leads to Christ first because the one it finally praises is not the woman but the fear of the LORD, and that fear is the beginning of everything Christ completes. Proverbs says it opens wisdom, Proverbs 9:10, and Isaiah says the coming Shoot of Jesse will delight in it, Isaiah 11:2-3. Jesus is the one in whom the fear of the LORD is perfect. He grew in wisdom, Luke 2:52, learned obedience, Hebrews 5:8, and in Gethsemane prayed that the Father's will be done, Matthew 26:39. The woman who fears the LORD is wise because of her reverence, and the one who bore that reverence without flaw is Christ.

It leads to Christ by the shape of Wisdom's story. Proverbs 1 to 9 introduces Wisdom as a person who calls out to the simple and offers a feast. Paul says that Christ is 'the power of God and the wisdom of God', 1 Corinthians 1:24, and that in Him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, Colossians 2:3. When this poem turns Wisdom into a laboring, giving, speaking person, it prepares the reader to recognise Wisdom made flesh. The Son who came to dwell among us, John 1:14, is the one in whom wisdom is perfectly lived out.

It leads to Christ in the details of service. The woman rises early to feed her household, verse 15; Jesus rose early to pray and to meet crowds, Mark 1:35. She opens her hands to the poor, verse 20; He fed the hungry, touched the leper and said that what was done for the least of His brothers was done for Him, Matthew 25:40. She speaks with faithful instruction, verse 26; of Him people said no one ever spoke the way He did, John 7:46. She is tired but strong; Jesus, weary from His journey, sat by a well, John 4:6, yet did not turn away the woman who came to it. Her life is poured out for others, and so was His, to the end, John 13:1.

It leads to Christ by the contrast between fading beauty and abiding worth. Verse 30 says charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting. Isaiah 53:2 says the Servant had no beauty that we should desire Him, yet His worth is greater than any other, and it is His abiding worth that Peter says is precious in God's sight when he speaks of the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, 1 Peter 3:4. In Christ, the person who fears the LORD is praised by God Himself.

A word of caution keeps the reading honest. The poem is about a human woman and a human household, and it is not coded talk about Jesus. The link to Christ rests on the New Testament's own claims about wisdom and the fear of the LORD, and on the pattern of a life of service that He fulfils. The poem tells women and men alike what a life that honours God looks like, and Christ is the one who lived it perfectly and who makes it possible for others to live it by His Spirit.
study.god:
The poem shows God by what He praises. The crowning line in verse 30 says that the one worth praising is the woman who fears the LORD, and the verb is the root of Hallelujah. God is the one who gives the standard for what is truly beautiful, and it is not what the world applauds. Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but reverence for Him lasts. A God who sets that standard is a God who looks at the heart, as He told Samuel in 1 Samuel 16:7.

It shows God as the giver of ordinary work. The poem is full of spinning, buying, cooking and planting, and it calls this the fruit of wisdom. God is not honoured only in temples and psalms; He is honoured in a field and a workshop. Paul says whatever you do, work at it with your whole being for the Lord, Colossians 3:23. The poem takes the six days of ordinary labour and gives them dignity.

It shows God as generous. The woman who opens her hands to the poor reflects the one who feeds the hungry and defends the cause of the poor. Proverbs 19:14 says a prudent wife is from the LORD, and Proverbs 18:22 that finding one brings favour from the LORD. The goodness of such a household is a gift from a gracious hand.

It shows God as the one who gives confidence about the future. Verse 25 says she can laugh at the days to come, not because she controls them but because she has lived rightly under the God who does. Psalm 112:1-3 has the same note for the one who fears the LORD. A God who can be trusted with tomorrow makes laughter possible today.

It shows the character of God as consistent. The fear of the LORD that opens Proverbs 1:7 also closes the book. There is no gap between the theology of the first chapter and the daily life of the last. The same God who is holy and awesome is the God who values a woman who is steady, kind and wise.

For worship, the poem teaches that praise belongs to what God has made and what God has made good. To fear the LORD is to learn to honour what He honours, in ourselves and others, and the response the poem asks for is exactly the verb it uses: to praise. Gratitude for faithful people, and a life that deserves the same word, is itself a kind of Hallelujah.

crossReferences.note: The man who finds wisdom is blessed, because she is more precious than rubies and nothing he desires compares with her. The poem opens by applying the same comparison to the woman of verse 10, so that the treasure of wisdom and the treasure of a wise wife are described in the same words.

Wisdom builds her house, prepares her table and sends out her maidservants. The woman of chapter 31 also builds a household, feeds it and directs maidservants, verse 15. The earlier passage shows wisdom as an invitation to the simple, and the poem shows it as a daily life.

A wife of noble character is her husband's crown, while one who shames him is like decay in his bones. It uses the same phrase as 31:10 and shows that the portrait at the end is built from an idea the book has been developing from the start.

Boaz tells Ruth that all his fellow townspeople know that she is a woman of noble character. The title is earned by a foreign widow through loyalty and work. It shows that the praise of the poem is not a privilege of rank but the reward of character.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. The book opens with this and Proverbs 31:30 closes with it, tying the whole collection into a single frame. Wisdom at the start is reverence, and wisdom at the end is a life that shows it.

Dorcas was always occupied with works of kindness and charity, and the widows showed Peter the clothes she had made. It is the poem lived out in a first-century congregation, with the needle and cloth of verse 19 and the open hand of verse 20.

The list of the good deeds expected of a widow, including bringing up children, hospitality, relief for the afflicted and devotion to every good work, is close to the poem's content. It shows the New Testament treating the same traits as marks of a godly woman.

Peter says beauty should come from the inner disposition of the heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit that is precious in God's sight. It restates verse 30 for the church, setting what fades against what God values.

Older women are to be teachers of good who train the young to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households and kind. It echoes the teaching tongue of verse 26 and the watchful care of verse 27, with the reason added: so that the word of God will not be discredited.

Jesus says a tree is known by its fruit. The poem ends by asking that the fruit of her hands be given to her and her works praise her at the gates. Both passages hold that wisdom and faith are proved by what they produce.

The bride of the Lamb has made herself ready and is given fine linen, bright and pure, which is the righteous acts of the saints. The fine linen of Proverbs 31:22 and the deeds that praise her at the gates reappear in the picture of the redeemed people.

Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, to present her glorious, holy and blameless. The poem about a capable wife is taken up by Paul in a picture of the church's life with Christ, and the husband's trust in verse 11 finds its answer in the Bridegroom's love.

study.oneStory:
The poem answers a question the Bible raises at the start. When God made the man and the woman, He called them to fill the earth and rule it, Genesis 1:28, and the woman was introduced as a strong helper, ezer, the word used elsewhere for God Himself as Israel's help, Genesis 2:18, Psalm 121:1-2. The fall damaged this partnership, with pain and struggle introduced into both work and marriage, Genesis 3:16-19. Proverbs 31 shows what that original calling looks like when wisdom restores it: work that is fruitful, trust between husband and wife, and a household that blesses the poor.

The poem also closes a thread inside Proverbs. The book opened with a father's voice warning against the loud woman Folly and urging the son to find Wisdom. It closes by showing what finding her looks like. The path of the fear of the LORD, which at the start seemed abstract, ends in a home, a market and a city gate.

As the story of Scripture goes on, the same character is seen in people. Ruth is the foreign woman who becomes a woman of noble character and enters David's line. Hannah's song and Mary's song show women whose reverence turns to praise. The early church includes Lydia, Dorcas, Priscilla and Phoebe, whose work in homes and congregations carries the poem forward. They are not perfect, and none of them is the whole poem, because the poem is a composite.

The story finds its centre in Christ, in whom wisdom is complete. He is the wisdom of God, and He builds a household, the church, and presents her to Himself without stain or wrinkle, Ephesians 5:27. The woman of Proverbs 31 is a faint preview of the bride who is made ready, and her works are matched by the righteous acts of the saints in Revelation 19:8. What the poem asks for, a life shaped by the fear of the LORD, becomes possible for ordinary people through the Spirit of Christ.

The new creation brings the outcome. The city descends like a bride adorned for her husband, Revelation 21:2, and the curse on labour and relationship is lifted. Work is no longer toil under thorns but service in the presence of God, and the praise given at the gates is joined to the praise of the nations. The woman who laughs at the days to come foreshadows a people who will have nothing left to fear.

sermon.title: A Woman Who Fears the Lord Is to Be Praised
sermon.why: Piper's message works directly from Proverbs 31:30 within the setting of the wider poem, Proverbs 31:10-31, drawing out how charm and beauty fade while reverence for the LORD is the one quality that finally deserves lasting praise, a fitting close to this study's emphasis on wisdom embodied and crowned by the fear of God.

quiz.q: What does verse 10 say about a wife of noble character?

options.text: She is far more precious than rubies.
options.note: Her worth is set above even the most valuable material treasure.

options.text: She is difficult to find but not especially valuable.
options.note: The verse explicitly calls her far more precious than rubies, a strong statement of value.

options.text: She is valuable mainly for her physical beauty.
options.note: The poem later explicitly ranks fearing the LORD above beauty, verse 30.

options.text: She is moderately valuable, similar to silver.
options.note: The comparison to rubies, among the most precious ancient gemstones, suggests far greater value than silver.

quiz.q: What activities does the poem highlight in verses 13 to 19?

options.text: Tireless, skillful labor, selecting wool and flax, rising early, buying a field, and spinning with her hands.
options.note: The poem repeatedly emphasizes diligent, capable work.

options.text: Leisure and rest as her primary daily activity.
options.note: This is the opposite of the tireless labor these verses describe.

options.text: Exclusively religious or ceremonial duties.
options.note: These verses focus on practical household and economic labor, not ceremonial duties.

options.text: Managing servants without doing any labor herself.
options.note: The verses specifically describe her own hands at work, not merely delegated management.

quiz.q: What does verse 20 say she does for the poor and needy?

options.text: She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy.
options.note: Generosity toward the vulnerable is a defining feature of her character.

options.text: She avoids contact with the poor to protect her family's wealth.
options.note: This is the opposite of the generosity described.

options.text: She gives to the poor only through official government channels.
options.note: The verse describes personal, direct generosity, not an institutional process.

options.text: She helps the poor only when it is convenient.
options.note: The verse gives no such qualification about convenience; her generosity is presented as a consistent practice.

quiz.q: According to verse 30, what does this poem ultimately hold up as worthy of praise?

options.text: A woman who fears the LORD, since charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting.
options.note: Reverence for God, not outward charm or beauty, is the poem's climactic praise.

options.text: Her physical beauty above all else.
options.note: The verse explicitly calls beauty fleeting, not the basis for lasting praise.

options.text: Her business success measured in wealth.
options.note: While her diligence is praised throughout, the explicit climax of verse 30 is fearing the LORD, not wealth.

options.text: Her charm and social skill.
options.note: The verse explicitly calls charm deceptive, the opposite of what deserves lasting praise.

quiz.q: How does verse 31 conclude the poem?

options.text: By calling for her to be given the fruit of her hands, and for her works to praise her at the gates.
options.note: Her own deeds, not merely words about her, are what publicly commend her.

options.text: By instructing her to remain silent about her accomplishments.
options.note: This is the opposite of the public praise the verse calls for.

options.text: By warning that her works will eventually be forgotten.
options.note: The verse calls for her works to praise her, implying lasting recognition, not forgetting.

options.text: By crediting her husband entirely for her accomplishments.
options.note: The verse specifically credits her own hands and works, not attributing them to her husband.

questions: This poem prizes strength, diligence, and generosity as marks of wisdom lived out. What is one concrete way you could embody wisdom more fully in your ordinary daily work this week?
Verse 20 highlights her open hands toward the poor and needy. Who is someone near you right now who could use practical generosity, and what is one specific thing you could give or do?
Verse 25 says she can laugh at the days to come, her strength and honor giving her security about the future. What fear about the future would change if you trusted more deeply in God's care?
Verse 30 says charm and beauty fade but the fear of the LORD is what truly deserves praise. Where are you currently investing more in appearance or charm than in a deepening reverence for God?

The poem closes by letting her own works praise her at the gates, verse 31. What would it look like for your life's quiet, faithful work, rather than your words about yourself, to be the thing that speaks loudest about your character?

translationNotes.note: 'Wife of noble character' translates eshet chayil, literally 'woman of strength or valor,' the same phrase used of Ruth in Ruth 3:11, and elsewhere applied to mighty warriors, framing this figure as strong and capable rather than merely decorative.

This whole section is an acrostic poem in Hebrew, its twenty-two lines beginning successively with each letter of the Hebrew alphabet from aleph to tav, a structural feature necessarily lost in translation but signaling a deliberately complete, idealized portrait.
'Charm is deceptive' can also be rendered 'charm is a lie' or 'grace is deceitful,' a strong Hebrew idiom underscoring how thoroughly outward charm can mislead about a person's true character.
